title: When do token systems stabilize? Compatibility constraints and community structure

paper.title: When do token systems stabilize? Compatibility constraints and community structure
paper.abstract:
Abstract Token systems support repeated service exchange without monetary transfers, but their viability depends on the stability of token balances.
We study token systems with compatibility constraints among agents.
A requester is randomly sampled in each period, and only a few randomly sampled agents are available to provide service.
We establish a necessary and sufficient condition for stability and show that the minimum-token rule, which selects the available provider with the lowest token balance, achieves the optimal stability region.
We then apply this stability criterion to a random token system generated from stochastic block models with uniformly sampled requesters.
We tightly characterize the stability regime by identifying two obstructions to stability: insufficient service opportunities for a group of communities or for an individual agent.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Token systems provide a way to organize repeated service exchange when monetary transfers are unavailable or undesirable. They have been implemented in babysitting cooperatives [ 61 ] , peer-to-peer systems [ 64 ] , and food banks [ 56 ] , among others. In a typical token system, an agent earns a token by providing a service and spends a token when receiving one. By recording past contributions, token systems provide a basis for sustaining cooperation and discouraging free riding when immediate or bilateral exchange is impractical. A key concern, however, is the stability of token balances: agents who accumulate large token balances may have little incentive to continue providing service. One application is cooperation between hospitals in kidney exchange. Pooling patient–donor pairs across hospitals creates opportunities for exchanges that individual hospitals could not arrange on their own. However, free riding has been documented in this setting: hospitals often match patient–donor pairs internally and submit primarily their harder-to-match pairs to centralized exchange platforms [ 7 , 4 , 8 ] . This selective participation motivates the use of token systems that account for hospitals’ contributions when assigning priority for future matching opportunities [ 6 ] ; see [ 32 ] for an earlier credit mechanism for multi-hospital kidney exchange. Motivated by this setting, [ 6 ] study a stochastic model of repeated service exchange among a finite set of agents. All agents start with a token balance of zero, and balances are allowed to become negative. In each discrete period, a randomly chosen agent requests service, and d d potential providers are sampled independently with replacement. These candidates represent the limited and fluctuating service opportunities available for a given request. Among the sampled candidates, the agent with the lowest token balance provides the service and receives one token from the requester. In the kidney-exchange interpretation, the requester is the hospital bringing an easy-to-match pair, while the potential providers are hospitals with compatible hard-to-match pairs. An exchange decreases the token balance of the hospital contributing the easy-to-match pair and increases that of the hospital whose hard-to-match pair is matched. Under this convention, a lower token balance corresponds to a larger net contribution to the shared pool. By giving hospitals with lower balances priority for matches involving their hard-to-match pairs, the minimum-token rule rewards past contributions and can encourage hospitals to contribute easy-to-match pairs to the shared pool. A central question for the viability of the system is whether token balances remain stable. Formally, stability means that the initial all-zero state is positive recurrent: the expected time of the first return to this state after time zero is finite. When both the requester and provider sampling distributions are uniform, [ 6 ] show that d = 1 d=1 leads to instability, whereas d = 2 d=2 already suffices for stability under the minimum-token rule. Thus, a choice between just two potential providers can suffice to stabilize the system. However, their model does not account for community structures in hospitals’ exchange relationships. Hospitals may, for example, restrict their partnerships to institutions with which they have previously cooperated, or institutions that are geographically close-by. In this paper, we study how such community structures affect the stability of token systems.

sections.heading: Our contributions.
sections.text: We generalize the model of [ 6 ] by sampling the d d potential providers independently with replacement from a requester-specific distribution. This notably captures compatibility constraints under which each agent can serve only a restricted subset of agents. We establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of an admissible stationary provider-selection rule that stabilizes the system ( Theorem 1 ). Informally, the condition compares each subset’s rate of requesting service with the probability that at least one of its members is sampled as a potential provider. We also show that the minimum-token rule, described in [ 6 ] as natural and motivated by incentive considerations, is optimal for stability: whenever an admissible stationary provider-selection rule stabilizes the system, the minimum-token rule does as well. In concurrent work, [ 43 ] obtains the corresponding characterization and optimality result when all requesters use the same strictly positive provider-sampling distribution. To understand how community structure affects stability, we specialize our general stability criterion to stochastic block models [ 34 , 1 , 2 ] , in which agents are partitioned into communities and compatibility links are generated with probabilities determined by community membership. We consider uniformly sampled requesters with d ≥ 2 d\geq 2 . We first identify two obstructions to stability: a community obstruction , when a group of communities has insufficient opportunities to provide service ( Proposition 1 ), and an individual obstruction , when a single agent has insufficient opportunities ( Proposition 2 ). We then show that excluding both obstructions guarantees stability with high probability ( Theorem 3 ). Our stability characterization covers all common degree scales: the individual obstruction is always present at sublogarithmic degree scales and, when the community condition holds, becomes vacuous at superlogarithmic degree scales, with the transition occurring at the logarithmic scale.

sections.heading: Token systems and service exchange.
sections.text: Many related models on token systems study service exchange with a fixed supply of tokens, often called scrip, and nonnegative balances. Requests may go unserved when the requester lacks the tokens needed to pay for service [ 26 , 40 , 41 , 37 ] . When agents maximize expected discounted benefits from receiving services net of the costs of providing them, [ 26 , 41 ] establish ε \varepsilon -Nash equilibria in sufficiently large populations of sufficiently patient agents, in which agents volunteer only when their token holdings fall below a threshold. [ 37 ] show that the minimum-scrip rule maximizes welfare among provider-selection rules in their homogeneous model. [ 39 ] study centralized control in such scrip systems. Their policy selects a compatible provider with the lowest balance and can reject requests to manage token circulation. It achieves asymptotically optimal welfare without knowing demand arrival rates. In a slightly different vein, [ 35 ] study favor trading with dynamic entry and exit, and design token issuance, redemption, and recycling mechanisms that can support an always-trade equilibrium. Their mechanism bounds token holdings and uses monetary transfers at balance boundaries and exit. Our model builds on [ 6 ] , where balances may be negative and have no imposed bounds. They show that the system is unstable with d = 1 d=1 , whereas the minimum-token rule ensures stability with d ≥ 2 d\geq 2 when requesters and candidate providers are sampled uniformly. They also give necessary and sufficient conditions for stability with two agents who may differ in their request and availability rates, assuming that candidate providers are sampled independently of the requester’s identity. In concurrent work, [ 43 ] characterizes the stability region for arbitrary strictly positive requester and provider distributions under this independence assumption, and also studies random service costs and stationary tail bounds. Our focus is on requester-specific compatibility constraints and stability in stochastic block models.

sections.heading: Kidney exchange.
sections.text: Credit mechanisms link successive matching rounds to encourage hospitals to disclose their patient–donor pairs [ 32 ] or to compensate countries whose past transplant allocations fell below a prescribed fair share [ 44 , 12 ] . The opportunities to provide such compensation are constrained by compatibility: hospitals and countries contribute pools that differ in size and composition [ 6 , 12 ] . Random-graph models capture this heterogeneity through directed compatibility edges between patient–donor pairs with type-dependent probabilities [ 7 , 5 ] . These features motivate our study of whether token systems can maintain balanced exchanges under heterogeneous compatibility constraints.

sections.heading: Other types of nonmonetary exchange and credit.
sections.text: Besides token systems, cooperation and allocation without money are studied through repeated favor exchange [ 51 , 33 , 3 ] , artificial currencies [ 31 , 30 ] , karma mechanisms [ 17 , 22 ] , and promises of future allocations [ 10 ] . In credit networks, payments are routed along trust-graph paths with enough residual credit [ 21 ] , possibly under per-agent borrowing caps [ 57 ] . Our graph instead restricts who can serve whom, and we study positive recurrence under nonstrategic selection rules rather than incentives, efficiency, or liquidity.

sections.heading: Load balancing and network constraints.
sections.text: The minimum-token rule is the greedy rule of the power of d d choices [ 49 ] , which sharply reduces delays in queueing [ 65 , 50 ] and maximum loads in balls-into-bins [ 9 ] . In the classical balls-into-bins model, the greedy rule is optimal among online d d -choice strategies, as the minimum-token rule is for stability. When candidate choices are constrained by a network, graphical variants draw candidates from a random edge [ 42 , 55 , 11 ] or a hypergraph-structured random set [ 29 ] . Compatibility-constrained queueing is studied through large-system limits [ 52 , 14 , 67 , 59 ] . In our model, the paying requester also determines the candidate distribution. Graphical allocation has also been studied with signed, conserved loads: in a synchronous model with uniform-vertex removals, [ 54 ] bound equilibrium load differences on connected regular graphs. In their asynchronous model, each arrival joins the (noisily) shortest nonnegative queue on its hyperedge, and an equilibrium exists if every vertex set serves faster than the hyperedges inside it receive arrivals. The strict form of our cut condition ( 1 ) gives the same subset-capacity inequality on complementary sets.

sections.heading: Queueing stability and scheduling.
sections.text: [ 62 ] give throughput-optimal scheduling policies for constrained queueing networks, and [ 63 ] show that serving the longest connected queue stabilizes parallel queues with random connectivity whenever any policy can. A complementary question is how to characterize the stability region through subset-capacity conditions. [ 25 ] show that Markovian join-the-shortest-queue routing within server subsets is positive recurrent if and only if every subset has more capacity than the demand confined to it. [ 20 ] recover this characterization via Lyapunov drift. Conditions of Hall type, similar to our cut condition, also arise in stochastic matching [ 16 ] . Match-the-longest is maximally stable in bipartite [ 15 ] and non-bipartite [ 47 ] matching models, as are generalized max-weight policies in the latter setting [ 38 ] .

sections.heading: Stochastic block models.
sections.text: Stochastic block models, rooted in social network analysis [ 34 , 66 ] , provide a simple framework for networks with community structure. Much of the literature [ 53 , 2 ] concerns recovering the blocks, for example by spectral clustering [ 46 ] . We instead use the model to generate compatibility constraints, as do [ 60 ] for online matching in a dense regime.

sections.heading: 3 Token systems with community structures
sections.text: Motivated by token systems where service opportunities can depend on social or organizational groups, a natural next step is to look at how common graph structures fare in terms of stability. For example, babysitting cooperatives may coordinate requests through separate sections [ 61 ] , while social clouds permit sharing within friendship networks or specified groups [ 18 ] . In addition, block structures have also been identified in time-bank transactions using stochastic block models [ 28 ] . We use a symmetric stochastic block model [ 34 , 1 , 2 ] to study how group-dependent service opportunities affect token-balance stability. After introducing the model in Section 3.1 , we show that stability with high probability is governed by two obstructions. We first describe the community obstruction in Section 3.2 : a group of whole communities requests service more often than at least one of its members appears among the available providers. We then describe the individual obstruction in Section 3.3 , where a single agent appears among the available providers less often than she requests service. To clearly convey the intuition behind individual obstructions, we start with Erdős–Rényi graphs in Section 3.3.1 , and then turn to the general stochastic block models in Section 3.3.2 . Finally, we show in Section 3.4 that the absence of both obstructions guarantees stability with high probability.

October 27, 2026 Abstract Token systems support repeated service exchange without monetary transfers, but their viability depends on the stability of token balances. We study token systems with compatibility constraints among agents. A requester is randomly sampled in each period, and only a few randomly sampled agents are available to provide service. We establish a necessary and sufficient condition for stability and show that the minimum-token rule, which selects the available provider with the lowest token balance, achieves the optimal stability region. We then apply this stability criterion to a random token system generated from stochastic block models with uniformly sampled requesters. We tightly characterize the stability regime by identifying two obstructions to stability: insufficient service opportunities for a group of communities or for an individual agent. 1 Introduction Token systems provide a way to organize repeated service exchange when monetary transfers are unavailable or undesirable. They have been implemented in babysitting cooperatives [ 61 ] , peer-to-peer systems [ 64 ] , and food banks [ 56 ] , among others. In a typical token system, an agent earns a token by providing a service and spends a token when receiving one. By recording past contributions, token systems provide a basis for sustaining cooperation and discouraging free riding when immediate or bilateral exchange is impractical. A key concern, however, is the stability of token balances: agents who accumulate large token balances may have little incentive to continue providing service. One application is cooperation between hospitals in kidney exchange. Pooling patient–donor pairs across hospitals creates opportunities for exchanges that individual hospitals could not arrange on their own. However, free riding has been documented in this setting: hospitals often match patient–donor pairs internally and submit primarily their harder-to-match pairs to centralized exchange platforms [ 7 , 4 , 8 ] . This selective participation motivates the use of token systems that account for hospitals’ contributions when assigning priority for future matching opportunities [ 6 ] ; see [ 32 ] for an earlier credit mechanism for multi-hospital kidney exchange. Motivated by this setting, [ 6 ] study a stochastic model of repeated service exchange among a finite set of agents. All agents start with a token balance of zero, and balances are allowed to become negative. In each discrete period, a randomly chosen agent requests service, and d d potential providers are sampled independently with replacement. These candidates represent the limited and fluctuating service opportunities available for a given request. Among the sampled candidates, the agent with the lowest token balance provides the service and receives one token from the requester. In the kidney-exchange interpretation, the requester is the hospital bringing an easy-to-match pair, while the potential providers are hospitals with compatible hard-to-match pairs. An exchange decreases the token balance of the hospital contributing the easy-to-match pair and increases that of the hospital whose hard-to-match pair is matched. Under this convention, a lower token balance corresponds to a larger net contribution to the shared pool. By giving hospitals with lower balances priority for matches involving their hard-to-match pairs, the minimum-token rule rewards past contributions and can encourage hospitals to contribute easy-to-match pairs to the shared pool. A central question for the viability of the system is whether token balances remain stable. Formally, stability means that the initial all-zero state is positive recurrent: the expected time of the first return to this state after time zero is finite. When both the requester and provider sampling distributions are uniform, [ 6 ] show that d = 1 d=1 leads to instability, whereas d = 2 d=2 already suffices for stability under the minimum-token rule. Thus, a choice between just two potential providers can suffice to stabilize the system. However, their model does not account for community structures in hospitals’ exchange relationships. Hospitals may, for example, restrict their partnerships to institutions with which they have previously cooperated, or institutions that are geographically close-by. In this paper, we study how such community structures affect the stability of token systems. Our contributions. We generalize the model of [ 6 ] by sampling the d d potential providers independently with replacement from a requester-specific distribution. This notably captures compatibility constraints under which each agent can serve only a restricted subset of agents. We establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of an admissible stationary provider-selection rule that stabilizes the system ( Theorem 1 ). Informally, the condition compares each subset’s rate of requesting service with the probability that at least one of its members is sampled as a potential provider. We also show that the minimum-token rule, described in [ 6 ] as natural and motivated by incentive considerations, is optimal for stability: whenever an admissible stationary provider-selection rule stabilizes the system, the minimum-token rule does as well. In concurrent work, [ 43 ] obtains the corresponding characterization and optimality result when all requesters use the same strictly positive provider-sampling distribution. To understand how community structure affects stability, we specialize our general stability criterion to stochastic block models [ 34 , 1 , 2 ] , in which agents are partitioned into communities and compatibility links are generated with probabilities determined by community membership. We consider uniformly sampled requesters with d ≥ 2 d\geq 2 . We first identify two obstructions to stability: a community obstruction , when a group of communities has insufficient opportunities to provide service ( Proposition 1 ), and an individual obstruction , when a single agent has insufficient opportunities ( Proposition 2 ). We then show that excluding both obstructions guarantees stability with high probability ( Theorem 3 ). Our stability characterization covers all common degree scales: the individual obstruction is always present at sublogarithmic degree scales and, when the community condition holds, becomes vacuous at superlogarithmic degree scales, with the transition occurring at the logarithmic scale. 1.1 Related literature Token systems and service exchange. Many related models on token systems study service exchange with a fixed supply of tokens, often called scrip, and nonnegative balances. Requests may go unserved when the requester lacks the tokens needed to pay for service [ 26 , 40 , 41 , 37 ] . When agents maximize expected discounted benefits from receiving services net of the costs of providing them, [ 26 , 41 ] establish ε \varepsilon -Nash equilibria in sufficiently large populations of sufficiently patient agents, in which agents volunteer only when their token holdings fall below a threshold. [ 37 ] show that the minimum-scrip rule maximizes welfare among provider-selection rules in their homogeneous model. [ 39 ] study centralized control in such scrip systems. Their policy selects a compatible provider with the lowest balance and can reject requests to manage token circulation. It achieves asymptotically optimal welfare without knowing demand arrival rates. In a slightly different vein, [ 35 ] study favor trading with dynamic entry and exit, and design token issuance, redemption, and recycling mechanisms that can support an always-trade equilibrium. Their mechanism bounds token holdings and uses monetary transfers at balance boundaries and exit. Our model builds on [ 6 ] , where balances may be negative and have no imposed bounds. They show that the system is unstable with d = 1 d=1 , whereas the minimum-token rule ensures stability with d ≥ 2 d\geq 2 when requesters and candidate providers are sampled uniformly. They also give necessary and sufficient conditions for stability with two agents who may differ in their request and availability rates, assuming that candidate providers are sampled independently of the requester’s identity. In concurrent work, [ 43 ] characterizes the stability region for arbitrary strictly positive requester and provider distributions under this independence assumption, and also studies random service costs and stationary tail bounds. Our focus is on requester-specific compatibility constraints and stability in stochastic block models. Kidney exchange. Credit mechanisms link successive matching rounds to encourage hospitals to disclose their patient–donor pairs [ 32 ] or to compensate countries whose past transplant allocations fell below a prescribed fair share [ 44 , 12 ] . The opportunities to provide such compensation are constrained by compatibility: hospitals and countries contribute pools that differ in size and composition [ 6 , 12 ] . Random-graph models capture this heterogeneity through directed compatibility edges between patient–donor pairs with type-dependent probabilities [ 7 , 5 ] . These features motivate our study of whether token systems can maintain balanced exchanges under heterogeneous compatibility constraints. Other types of nonmonetary exchange and credit. Besides token systems, cooperation and allocation without money are studied through repeated favor exchange [ 51 , 33 , 3 ] , artificial currencies [ 31 , 30 ] , karma mechanisms [ 17 , 22 ] , and promises of future allocations [ 10 ] . In credit networks, payments are routed along trust-graph paths with enough residual credit [ 21 ] , possibly under per-agent borrowing caps [ 57 ] . Our graph instead restricts who can serve whom, and we study positive recurrence under nonstrategic selection rules rather than incentives, efficiency, or liquidity. Load balancing and network constraints. The minimum-token rule is the greedy rule of the power of d d choices [ 49 ] , which sharply reduces delays in queueing [ 65 , 50 ] and maximum loads in balls-into-bins [ 9 ] . In the classical balls-into-bins model, the greedy rule is optimal among online d d -choice strategies, as the minimum-token rule is for stability. When candidate choices are constrained by a network, graphical variants draw candidates from a random edge [ 42 , 55 , 11 ] or a hypergraph-structured random set [ 29 ] . Compatibility-constrained queueing is studied through large-system limits [ 52 , 14 , 67 , 59 ] . In our model, the paying requester also determines the candidate distribution. Graphical allocation has also been studied with signed, conserved loads: in a synchronous model with uniform-vertex removals, [ 54 ] bound equilibrium load differences on connected regular graphs. In their asynchronous model, each arrival joins the (noisily) shortest nonnegative queue on its hyperedge, and an equilibrium exists if every vertex set serves faster than the hyperedges inside it receive arrivals. The strict form of our cut condition ( 1 ) gives the same subset-capacity inequality on complementary sets. Queueing stability and scheduling. [ 62 ] give throughput-optimal scheduling policies for constrained queueing networks, and [ 63 ] show that serving the longest connected queue stabilizes parallel queues with random connectivity whenever any policy can. A complementary question is how to characterize the stability region through subset-capacity conditions. [ 25 ] show that Markovian join-the-shortest-queue routing within server subsets is positive recurrent if and only if every subset has more capacity than the demand confined to it. [ 20 ] recover this characterization via Lyapunov drift. Conditions of Hall type, similar to our cut condition, also arise in stochastic matching [ 16 ] . Match-the-longest is maximally stable in bipartite [ 15 ] and non-bipartite [ 47 ] matching models, as are generalized max-weight policies in the latter setting [ 38 ] . Stochastic block models. Stochastic block models, rooted in social network analysis [ 34 , 66 ] , provide a simple framework for networks with community structure. Much of the literature [ 53 , 2 ] concerns recovering the blocks, for example by spectral clustering [ 46 ] .
